title: Why can one narrow strait move your gas price?

record.question: Why can one narrow strait move your gas price?
record.audience_reason: Hormuz is in the oil news all year and gas prices touch everyone; the puzzle (the U.S. imports only 8% of its crude from the Gulf) makes the global-market mechanism click.

editorial_contribution.statement: We connect a pump price to a strait the viewer will never see: a to-scale bar of 2025 U.S. crude imports (8% from the Gulf), the 2024 flow through Hormuz (~20 million b/d, about a fifth of world use), a labeled what-if in which bypass pipelines (EIA estimate ~2.6 million b/d available) carry only a sliver, and a simplified one-market board where Asian buyers bid for other barrels and every price meter, Texas included, rises together; crude is about half of a gallon's price.

record.custom_scene: A simplified dusk map of the strait with a dashed tanker lane and a yellow tanker to track; a red barrier closes the narrow part, tankers queue, two teal bypass pipelines carry a thin flow over land while a to-scale bar shows ~2.6 of 20 million b/d; then a four-region market board (Asia, Europe, Texas, Africa) where Asia's orange bid arrows reach every other region and linked price meters rise together until Texas lights up; a to-scale gallon bar puts crude at about half; a receipt prints beside the jammed strait.

cover_composition.main_object: tankers squeezing through the simplified strait with a gas pump showing a yellow up arrow

record.sources_and_assumptions: See sources-and-rights.md. Assumptions: the closure is a labeled hypothetical, not a description of current traffic or a forecast; we avoid any current-year traffic numbers. '8%' is EIA's Middle East Gulf share of 2025 U.S. crude imports; '20 million b/d / about 20%' is EIA's 2024 figure (IEA gives 20 mb/d for 2025); bypass ~2.6 million b/d is EIA's estimate of available unused Saudi+UAE pipeline capacity (IEA gives 3.5-5.5 mb/d of capacity), narrated as 'a few million'; 'about half' = crude's share of the 2025 retail gasoline price (EIA chart ~51%; API citing EIA 'about 51%'). The market board and meters are illustrative (no prices shown). The map is simplified, not to scale.
record.asset_provenance: All visuals drawn in code (Pillow) for this episode: simplified map, generic tankers, pump, barrels, receipt; no logos, no real people. Inter (OFL); narration Kokoro (Apache-2.0); sound effects and music bed synthesized (templates/sfx.py).

explain.understand: if the strait is blocked, pipelines can't replace most of the flow

explain.change: the lane closes; a thin teal flow continues on land; most volume stays behind
text: spare pipelines: ~2.6 of 20 million b/d (EIA est.)

scenes.tts: Now imagine it gets choked. Spare pipelines around it could reroute only a few million barrels a day... the rest is stuck.

scenes.subject: simplified market board: Asia, Europe, Texas, Africa with barrels and meters; Asia's bid arrows reach the others

explain.understand: buyers who lose Gulf oil compete for oil from other places
explain.objects: four region cards, barrels, price meters, bid arrows
explain.change: arrows extend from Asia to every other region
explain.cause: lost supply has to be replaced from the same pool
text: 84% of the strait's crude went to Asia (2024)
Asian buyers bid for other barrels

scenes.tts: Most of it was headed to Asia. Those buyers bid for barrels everywhere else.

scenes.subject: same board: a link line joins the meters, every meter rises at once, Texas outlined in yellow

explain.understand: oil prices around the world move together, so U.S. crude rises too
explain.change: all meters rise; Texas lights up
explain.cause: crude trades in a global market; prices of crude streams tend to move together

scenes.tts: Crude trades in one global market. So prices rise together. Even in Texas.
